qs.q: What is the most common and serious congenital bladder anomaly that predisposes patients to ascending pyelonephritis?
qs.e: Vesicoureteral reflux is the most common and serious congenital bladder anomaly, directly predisposing to ascending pyelonephritis and loss of renal function. Diverticula are pouch-like invaginations that typically cause urinary stasis and calculi rather than primary reflux.
qs.s: DISORDERS OF THE LOWER URINARY TRACT — Revision Notes — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: What is the most common route of infection in pyelonephritis?
qs.e: The note states that 'Ascending — most common route' is how infection reaches the kidney in pyelonephritis. Hematogenous spread is mentioned as less common.
qs.s: Acute Tubular Injury (ATI): AKI Causes, Pathology & Prognosis — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following conditions is a classic setting for papillary necrosis, a complication of acute pyelonephritis?
qs.e: Diabetes mellitus is listed as one of the 'Classic settings' for papillary necrosis, along with sickle cell disease and urinary tract obstruction. Hypertension, SLE, and glomerulonephritis are not mentioned in this context.
qs.s: Acute Tubular Injury (ATI): AKI Causes, Pathology & Prognosis — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: What is a key diagnostic clue for chronic pyelonephritis, distinguishing it from other kidney diseases?
o: Symmetric scarring of the renal cortex
Involvement of the calyces and pelvis
qs.e: The note emphasizes that 'only chronic pyelonephritis and analgesic nephropathy affect the calyces — pelvocalyceal damage is a diagnostic clue'. Glomerulonephritis causes symmetric scarring, and TIN is characterized by interstitial inflammation.
qs.s: Acute Tubular Injury (ATI): AKI Causes, Pathology & Prognosis — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following is a characteristic symptom of pyelonephritis?
qs.e: Pyelonephritis is characterized by symptoms such as abdominal, back, or flank pain, and fever. Dysuria, frequency, and suprapubic pain are more indicative of cystitis.

qs.q: Which age group is at the highest risk for developing acute pyelonephritis and subsequent renal scarring after a febrile UTI?
o: Children six months to two years
qs.e: Children younger than 2 years of age are at the highest risk for developing acute pyelonephritis and subsequent renal scarring following a febrile UTI. While children of any age can be affected, the risk is significantly elevated in this younger group.

qs.q: Which of the following clinical features is characteristic of acute pyelonephritis rather than uncomplicated cystitis?
qs.e: Acute pyelonephritis is suggested by prominent systemic symptoms with fever, rigors, vomiting, hypotension, and loin pain, guarding, or tenderness. Cystitis features are primarily localized to suprapubic pain, frequency, urgency, and dysuria.

qs.q: A 23-year-old woman with recurrent UTIs, at least one episode of pyelonephritis. Blood typing shows the P blood group antigen. Likely primary cause of her infections
o: Escherichia coli O157:H7 (LPS O antigen 157; flagellar antigen H7)
Escherichia coli with K1 (capsular type 1) antigen
qs.e: P-pili (fimbriae) bind to a receptor related to the P blood group antigen on uroepithelial cells, mediating attachment and ascending infection to the kidneys (pyelonephritis).
qs.s: Medical Bacteriology MCQs: Review Strep, TB, Anthrax & More

ai.summary: Pyelonephritis is an infection of the kidney’s collecting system, usually ascending from the bladder. It presents with fever, flank pain and urinary symptoms, and requires prompt antibiotics and supportive care.

sections.p: Acute pyelonephritis is a bacterial infection of the renal parenchyma and pelvis, most often caused by E. coli ascending from the bladder. Diagnosis combines clinical features, urine culture and imaging when available.

sections.p: The most common cause is ascending E. coli infection. Other bacteria include Klebsiella, Proteus, and in low‑resource settings, organisms linked to HIV, TB, or malaria.
Patients report fever, chills, flank pain, and urinary urgency. In children, symptoms may be nonspecific, with irritability and poor feeding.
Tests confirm infection, identify the organism, and assess severity. When resources are limited, clinical judgment and basic labs guide treatment.
